extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students/scholars of poetics and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance (Aristotelian) on composing and evaluating poetic and dramatic works: metaphor, diction, metre, unity of plot, use of the marvelous, and appropriate stylistic licences across genres (epic, tragedy, iambic, dithyramb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of metaphor / analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor may proceed from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy/proportion — e.g., 'There lies my ship' (lying at anchor a species of lying); 'ten thousand' for a large number; or proportion where the second term is to the first as the fourth to the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use different operative kinds of metaphor deliberately (genus↔species, species↔species, proportion). Examples: calling the cup 'the shield of Dionysus' (cup : Dionysus :: shield : Ares); or using 'sowing' for the sun's scattering of rays. These substitutions must respect resemblance relations; they are acceptable modes of metaphorical naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified/extended metaphor use
rubrics_metrics.description: You may qualify a metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative, or apply an alien term and then deny of that term one of its proper attributes (e.g., call the shield not 'the cup of Ares' but 'the wineless cup').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor can be clarified by appending the referent (making relations explicit). One may also use an alien term and negate some of its usual attributes to produce effect. Use these techniques sparingly and with attention to intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel coinage
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never been even in local use, but is invented by the poet himself (examples: ἐρνύγες 'sprouters' for κέρατα 'horns'; ἀρητήρ 'supplicator' for ἱερεύς 'priest').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coinage is permissible and can be effective, but it is a marked device. Invented words should be used when they illuminate resemblance or produce distinction; avoid excessive coinage that produces jargon or obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word modification: lengthening/contracting/alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is lengthened when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or a syllable inserted; contracted when part is removed; altered when part retains ordinary form and part is re-cast (examples of lengthening and contraction are given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthening, contraction, and partial alteration can give diction distinction while preserving perspicuity when there remains partial conformity with common usage. These licences contribute to an elevated but still clear style if used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of clarity and loftiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style uses current or proper words (but may be mean); a lofty style is raised above the common-place by strange/rare/metaphorical/lengthened forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a mix: proper/current words give perspicuity; rare/metaphorical/ornamental words raise diction. Purely current diction may be too 'mean'; wholly unusual diction becomes riddle or jargon. Seek an equilibrium that preserves understanding while achieving elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation to avoid riddle or jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of strange (or rare) words is either a riddle (if metaphors) or a jargon (if strange words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an infusion of unusual elements (metaphor, rare words, ornamental forms) but avoid making them the whole of diction. Anti-patterns: entire passages made of metaphors (riddle) or rare terms (jargon) which obscure sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate use of linguistic licences
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ licences (lengthening, rare words, metaphors, exotic forms) obtrusively is grotesque; moderation is necessary in any mode of poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert stylistic deviations merely to show off; they must serve the work's effect. Excessive or conspicuous manipulation of form risks ludicrousness or triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction to genre and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of words suit different genres: compound words are best for dithyrambs, rare words for heroic poetry, metaphors for iambic; in iambic verse (which reproduces familiar speech) words found in prose are most appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diction according to genre and metre: heroic (epic) admits rare words and metaphors; iambic favors prose-like, familiar language; dithyrambic allows compounds. Genre-specific appropriateness is crucial: mismatched register is an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative imitation in single metre should have a plot constructed on dramatic principles: a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, middle, and end, producing the appropriate pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose plots that represent one coherent action rather than a series of loosely related events. Anti-patterns: treating a period of events (many incidents at the same time) as if they formed a single dramatic action; overcomplication that prevents a single view of beginning and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope/length to medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from Tragedy in scale; the beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view. Epic has capacity for great enlargement but should answer in length to the group of tragedies presented at one sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope that allows the audience/reader to apprehend the work as a whole. Excessive vastness makes the poem unmanageable; epic may be larger than tragedy but still must maintain coherence of beginning and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes to diversify without breaking unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes (e.g., Catalogue of ships) may be admitted to diversify the poem but should not undermine the unity of the single action selected (Homer detaches a portion and admits episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include episodes insofar as they enrich and diversify without deranging the central unity. Episodes should relate to and support the main action, not replace or fragment it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre selection and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure is the stateliest and most massive and is therefore especially fit for epic; iambic and trochaic tetrameters suit other functions (trochaic akin to dancing, iambic expressive of action). Mixing metres (as Chaeremon did) is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the metre that suits the genre and keep metrical consistency for large-scale works. Avoid arbitrary mixing of metres which produces incongruity and weakens the formal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal authorial intrusion & character distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; instead introduce persons with characteristic qualities and distinct characters (Homer brings in a man or woman 'none of them wanting in characteristic qualities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor dramatized presentation over authorial explanation. Characters should be introduced through action and speech that reveal distinctive ethos; excessive authorial narration diminishes imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility: handling marvelous and irrational elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The element of the wonderful is admissible (especially in epic), but the irrational should, if possible, be excluded from the dramatic action or lie outside it; when absurdities occur they must be veiled by poetic charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct events to seem plausible within the poem's means of belief: choose 'probable impossibilities' (things that could be believed given the context) rather than outright implausibilities. In drama, keep irrational incidents out of the acting parts; in narrative forms, poetic narration can obscure absurdity but this requires skill. Anti-pattern: plots composed of irrational parts that make the whole ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate placement of elaborate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought; conversely, over-brilliant diction obscures character and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate, dazzling language for moments that do not convey character or critical thought; during decisive action or moments of character-revelation prefer clarity. Anti-pattern: using highly ornate diction when the scene requires psychological or ethical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor (quality) as mark of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing is to have a command of metaphor; to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances and cannot be imparted by another—it is the mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metaphors for aptness of resemblance and imaginative perception rather than mere ornament. High-quality metaphorical thinking is a central criterion of poetic excellence; training helps technique, but the evaluative standard is the poet's ability to see and transfer likenesses apt for the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of 'errors' vs acceptable impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between faults intrinsic to the art and accidental faults. If an impossibility arises from the nature of the art's limits or the poem's end it may not be an error; if it prevents the end or violates the art's proper capacities then it is an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging apparent impossibilities, determine whether they frustrate the work's end or lie within what the art may permissibly represent. Example: if the 'end' could not have existed given the medium and the poet nonetheless required it, that's blameworthy; but if the impossibility does not vitiate the work's end it may be tolerable.
